How independent safety testing helped Neuly achieve medical device status — Fault Line Fault Line Approach Research Blog About Book a call Approach Research Blog About Book a call → ← Blog Company 21 October 2026 How independent safety testing helped Neuly achieve medical device status How Fault Line built Neuly's medical device risk register, enabling it to become one of the first generative AI parenting tools registered as a medical device. Ben Carrington Co-CEO Contents At a glance The challenge About Neuly Why Fault Line Building the medical device evidence Optimising product performance & safety quickly Independence that builds confidence What’s next 7,500+ adversarial conversations 22 clinical risk dimensions tested 6 weeks from start to medical device submission At a glance Within two weeks of integrating, Fault Line had built the backbone of Neuly’s medical device risk register by running thousands of adversarial conversations against the world’s most comprehensive clinical AI risk taxonomy . Neuly used the results to strengthen the product before launch and become one of the first generative AI parenting support tools for families of neurodivergent children to be registered as a medical device. The challenge Generative AI is moving into regulated healthcare faster than the methods for proving it is safe. Traditional medical device validation assumes predictable outputs from known inputs. Generative AI breaks this model because it can answer the same question or perform the same task differently each time. Its behaviour and performance can also differ whenever its prompt, scaffolding or underlying model changes. Whilst regulators figure out a path forward, clinical AI companies seeking medical device status face two options: Shoehorn generative AI into traditional risk evaluation, verification & validation and post-market surveillance methodologies that won’t survive regulatory scrutiny. Compensate for the stochasticity by running testing and/or clinical studies at such high sample sizes that the cost and time requirements are untenable and can’t be kept up post-market. Neuly chose a third path: put its AI through medical device aligned independent adversarial testing. That sets a high bar for safety. “We had controls in place to identify and flag risky conversations. What we didn’t have was a way to test how the product behaves at scale before a single parent used it, across situations we couldn’t script ourselves, and a method for turning what we found into concrete improvements. Fault Line gave us both.” — Deepthi Uppala, CTO & Co-Founder, Neuly About Neuly Neuly is an AI coach for parents and carers of neurodivergent children. Through voice and text conversations, it helps families understand their child, work through everyday challenges and build strategies that fit their child’s needs, alongside any professional support the family already has. Neuly remembers each child’s profile across sessions, so its guidance becomes more personal over time. The team behind Neuly has spent years in paediatric ADHD and autism support. Their users are often parents at the end of a long day, worried about a child they love. The company cares deeply about user safety and building a product that keeps parents coming back to it. Why Fault Line Neuly chose to work with Fault Line because the team has been where Neuly is. The founders led the regulatory strategy, clinical AI research and commercial rollout of the world’s first AI mental health chatbot to earn Class IIa medical device status in the UK. That product has since assessed more than 650,000 patients and is used by nearly half of NHS Talking Therapies services. The team knows what regulators ask for, what evidence holds up and where generative AI breaks traditional validation methods. That experience sits alongside more than 34 academic publications and 1,300 citations in clinical AI research, and a decade of shipping production machine learning in healthcare. Fault Line is also at the forefront of how generative AI medical devices will be regulated. Fault Line has turned that experience into a platform for independent, scientifically rigorous evaluation, monitoring and optimisation of clinical AI. Clinical and product teams stress test their AI agents with the most comprehensive clinical AI evaluation platform on the planet , and get back quantified, statistical measures of safety and performance that meet international regulation, governance and compliance standards. The two teams embarked on a partnership to build the safety evidence for Neuly’s medical device registration. Building the medical device evidence Fault Line worked alongside the Neuly team to run a series of medical device grade audits that became the backbone of the product’s risk management and post-market surveillance activities. Integration was quick. Neuly connected its AI to the Fault Line platform via API and the first audit was running the same week, baselining performance through thousands of adversarial conversations, with audit results providing a range of safety measures and risk controls for improving the product’s performance along specific risk dimensions. After the Neuly team implemented those controls, audits were re-run at scale to verify they were effective. The results were translated into ISO 14971 aligned risk scoring so the evidence could slot straight into the technical file without the team having to rework it. Fault Line’s methods and evidence now sit at the heart of the AI safety case in Neuly’s technical file, and Neuly has a repeatable process for keeping that evidence up to date as the product changes over time to support change control, post-market surveillance and ongoing performance monitoring. Updates to a medical device, such as a change of foundation model, can normally mean a lengthy re-evaluation. With the Fault Line platform, Neuly can generate the evidence for a product update within minutes. Optimising product performance & safety quickly For Neuly’s product team, the biggest day-to-day value was speed. The team needed to know quickly whether an edit made the product better or whether the change negatively impacted any specific performance sub-dimensions. A clinical AI product can behave differently across many situations after any change, whether to a prompt, the scaffolding around the model or the model itself. Without a reliable way to measure the effect, it’s a guess which behaviours a change has affected and what testing it needs. This often slows down development, pitting clinical and product teams against each other in a tension between shipping fast and shipping safely. The Fault Line platform turned that into a tight loop. Each audit came with targeted safety improvements tied to the specific risk and performance dimensions they were designed to address, so the team could see exactly what to change and why. The Neuly team could review the improvements and deploy them the same day. Running targeted mini-audits on the relevant risk dimensions then showed within a couple of hours whether the change had worked. Because the platform can also load in product-specific evals and performance classifiers, the Neuly team could also check that an update hadn’t adversely impacted usability or made the product less helpful to the parents using it. That meant Neuly could make several rounds of improvements in a fraction of the time a single round of manual testing would normally take. Every change was measured against the same baseline, so the team could statistically compare versions with confidence intervals directly and move forward with confidence. “Integration was ready within days. The audits came back with specific recommendations tied to named risk dimensions, so we could change the prompt, re-run the relevant tests and see the effect the same day. A quantified score against a fixed baseline took the argument out of release decisions.” — Laura Douglas, Lead AI Engineer, Neuly Independence that builds confidence The independent nature of Fault Line testing gives the Neuly team confidence to ship knowing that every release can be measured and checked against a clinically grounded set of risks that is always up to date with the latest findings, research and publications in clinical AI safety . Beyond the impact on product improvements and medical device evidence, the independence Fault Line provides has also become a useful asset in external commercial, partnership and investor conversations. Independent evaluation against an explainable, scientifically grounded methodology gives those stakeholders a transparent view of how the product performs against clinical risks. “Partners and investors ask the same question: how has this been tested? Pointing to independent adversarial testing against a published clinical risk taxonomy, with a methodology we can explain line by line, is a much stronger answer than describing our own internal checks.” — Deepthi Uppala, CTO & Co-Founder, Neuly What’s next Following the medical device project, Neuly and Fault Line have agreed to expand their work together to more tightly integrate the Fault Line platform into Neuly’s software lifecycle process and build out more materials to support Neuly’s governance, compliance and commercial conversations. Fault Line AI, London, UK 2. Sydney Medical School, University of Sydney, Sydney, Australia 3. AI Security Institute, London, UK 4. Wolfson Institute of Population Health, Queen Mary University of London, London, United Kingdom 5. Institute for Human-Centered AI, Helmholtz Munich, Munich, Germany 6. Department of Psychiatry, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK 7. Max Planck UCL Centre for Computational Psychiatry and Ageing Research, London, UK Description As large language models are more frequently used for clinical and wellbeing purposes, the regulatory and clinical scrutiny increases, requiring AI manufacturers to provide proof that they tested all possible risks. Current taxonomies and benchmarks are handcrafted by experts, ultimately representing the (subjective) perspective of the authors. As the literature on clinical AI safety grows rapidly, the field has become fragmented and no single taxonomy covers the entire risk space. The field lacks a unified and objective taxonomy that covers the full diversity of potential risks of clinical AI, scales alongside the growing literature, and allows the quantification of sufficient safety testing. We present FAULT (Factor Analytic Unification of Literature Taxonomy), built through a data-driven pipeline characterising clinical AI risks. We produce an automated pipeline summarising the scientific literature, finding 139 unique clinical AI failure modes. We then investigated the co-occurrence of these failure modes across 14,232 health-related real-world and benchmark data using factor analysis, revealing that these failure modes can be condensed into 22 risk dimensions due to overlap in the constructs. Importantly, analysing existing benchmarks with this taxonomy indicates that no individual benchmark covers the full risk spectrum of clinical risks. Finally, we conduct an epidemiological analysis of the prevalence of these risk dimensions across 132,505 benchmark and real-world conversations, illustrating that current benchmarks lack representativeness for clinical risks as it presents in the real-world. Our work provides a novel approach for defining a taxonomy of clinical AI risks in a data-driven way which enables quantification of what sufficient safety testing looks like for clinical AI, and provides a standardised blueprint for future safety benchmarks.
